newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU, Spain hopeful for Unisource, telecoms deal.
newsitem.headline: EU, Spain hopeful for Unisource, telecoms deal.

text.p: The European Commission and Spain made little progress on Wednesday on the opening of the Spanish telecommunications market to free competition, which holds the key to EU approval of the Unisource telecoms alliance.

But the two sides were optimistic that a compromise would be found, possibly before mid November, when the European Union is expected to improve its offer on telecoms market liberalisation at the World Trade Organisation.

"We are getting close to an agreement," a Spanish diplomat said after a meeting between Spanish Development Minister Rafael Arias Salgado, who is in charge of telecommunications, and Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert.
A Commission official confirmed that progress had been made, but said that Van Miert was still not entirely happy.

In a memorandum to the Commission, Spain formally committed itself to opening its market to full competition on January 1, 1998 -- the same date as all but a few smaller EU states -- thus waiving a hard-won five-year delay.
But if that initiative was a key achievement, the Commission wants to ensure that this does not happen on paper only.

"We still have a problem regarding effective liberalisation," the Commission official said. At issue was the granting of licences to allow new operators to compete with partly state-owned Telefonica de Espana.

The Commission has asked for an early opening of the Spanish telecoms markets in return for its approval of the Unisource alliance between telecoms operators Dutch PTT, Telia AB of Sweden and Swiss Telecom PTT on the one hand and Telefonica on the other hand.
The EU is also vetting a joint venture between Unisource and giant U.S. telecoms operator AT&T Corp called Uniworld.

Like other telecoms alliances, the Unisource and Uniworld deals are designed to take advantage of the break-up of national monopolies in Europe as well as to offer value-added services on a global scale.

Spain's reluctance to give up its five-year delay to the 1998 EU deadline is also undermining multilateral talks on telecoms liberalisation at the WTO which negotiators are hoping to conclude early in 1997.
In the memorandum presented to the Commission on Wednesday, Spain proposed to grant telecoms licences from 1999. But Van Miert was quoted by the official as saying that this was "unacceptable".
Under EU rules, 1998 is the deadline for telecoms liberalisation, not the beginning. Van Miert did not say when he wished to see Spain granting licences.
Besides Telefonica, there is already a second state-controlled telecoms operator in Spain called Retevision, which operates cable television, digital radio and satellite communications services.
Retevision is up for sale with potential candidates including Deutsche Telekom and Global One, the joint venture between Telekom, France Telecom and Sprint Corp.
